title: Dimapur horticulture & floriculture: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**This is a living-asset business: cuttings and seedlings go into protected or open beds, and cash comes back only when a stem or seedling is sold within days of harvest.** Orchids, gerbera and carnation have been grown successfully in Nagaland, and the district administration and Central Institute of Horticulture, Medziphema have pushed protected and open cultivation with market linkages [1]. A hi-tech vegetable seedlings unit already sits at the State Horticulture Nursery, Dimapur [2]. **The value sits in the last mile — grading, cold chain and the buyer — not in the field.** Post-harvest handling of flowers and losses of horticultural produce were the core training topics at SAMETI, Medziphema [3].

## Where cash and risk sit
**Working capital is short and brutal: flowers are perishable, so a missed sale is a write-off, not inventory.** The Horticulture Commissioner flagged the need for flower-drying technology, which tells you spoilage is the live problem [1]. **Capex is polyhouse and nursery structure — long-lived, loan-funded, and only worth it if the buyer contract outlives the loan.** Note the age of our local file: the training report is dated July 2020 and the seedlings unit January 2018 [1][2], so treat both as background, not current market evidence. **Dimapur-specific price, yield and buyer data is thin — collect from customer.**

## What peers say
**Peer results are split, and that is the real signal.** Pushpanjali Floriculture grew March 2026 net sales to Rs 13.18 crore, up 40.95% from Rs 9.35 crore, yet posted a quarterly net loss of Rs 2.15 crore and negative EBITDA of Rs 0.24 crore [6]. Nagarjuna Agri-Tech's June 2026 quarter shows sales of INR 321.81 million against INR 15.31 million a year ago [5], with margin slippage as interest and depreciation rose [7]. **Volume growth without margin is the pattern — so when a proposal lands, check EBITDA margin and interest cover, not turnover; if sales are growing but EBITDA is negative, ask what the price realisation per stem actually is.**

## Who to pursue now
**Pursue the seedling and planting-material producer first** — it sells a repeat input to other growers, has a shorter cash cycle than cut flowers, and the Dimapur nursery precedent exists [2]. **Second, protected-cultivation flower growers with a written buyer tie-up**, since the district machinery has explicitly backed protected cultivation with market linkages [1]. **Avoid open-field cut-flower growers selling into spot markets and anyone without a cold-chain or drying plan** — spoilage risk sits entirely on us [1][3].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the crop cycle, not the loan tenor.** Take monthly stock-and-sales statements, and a monthly sweep of sale proceeds through the account. **Take a charge on the polyhouse and a post-dated cheque for each harvest season; if receivables age past one cycle, ask for the buyer's payment record.** Insist on crop insurance and a named buyer before disbursal.

## Early warning signs
- **Spoilage or rejection reported at the buyer end** — pull the limit and re-assess within the month.
- **Sales up but EBITDA negative, as in the peer case [6]** — stop fresh disbursal and ask for cost breakup.
- **No buyer contract renewal on file** — treat as unsecured and reduce exposure.
watch: Spoilage or rejection above normal -> freeze limit and inspect the packhouse
Proceeds routed outside the account -> ask for buyer payment proof and re-rate
EBITDA and interest cover from quarterly returns (quarterly)
Sales up but EBITDA negative -> stop fresh disbursal, seek cost breakup
No renewal on file -> treat exposure as unsecured and reduce
Lapse or charge not perfected -> withhold next tranche
